(Gausby, 2015) a report by Microsoft, explores trends in attention spans where 
in the year 2000 the average attention span was around 12 seconds, and in 
2013 this has gone down to 8 seconds. Figure 2, shows that reduced attention 
spans seem to be worse with younger generations, and is highly correlated with 
high levels of media consumption and social media usage. 
2.3.3 Microlearning Educational framework 
From these trends it may be easy to conclude that simply stopping younger 
generations from using social-media and instant gratification platforms would 
resolve the issue. However, this of course is unrealistic, Microlearning attempts 
to mimic recent trends towards shorter content consumption, by itself breaking 
down topics into small bite size chunks (Lindner, 2007).  
By having smaller lessons, microlearning can help improve student engagement 
(Liao, et al., 2017; Nikou & Economides, 2018). An exact length of video or 
lesson is not widely agreed upon; however most papers agree on a length 
between 5-15 minutes (Barana, et al., 2019; Brame, 2016; Ilona & Henrike, 
2010). In fact an article by (Zaveri, 2023), claims that 50% of TikTok users find 
videos over one minute stressful; and with 74% of 16-to-17 year olds using the 
platform (Ofcom, 2022), there might now be a bias towards shorter bursts of 
information. A possible hybrid approach could have a series of sub one-minute 
clips, culminating into a 5–15-minute lesson. 
A meta-analysis by (Taylor & Hung, 2022), found that microlearning had highly 
positive effects over traditional learning methods with: (1) 62% of studies 
finding positive effects on task-based performance objectives (2) 38% of studies 
finding positive effects in knowledge retention (3) microlearning groups were 
found to outperform control groups at skill acquisition and had improved pass 
rates.
